title: Do You Own Your Enterprise Cortex? The AI Strategy Risk CEOs May Not See Coming.
gist: BCG names a new enterprise AI risk it calls cognitive lock-in: as models and agents become part of how a company reasons, its data, rules, and operational context fuse to one provider's stack until switching is prohibitive — and contracts cannot protect judgment the way they protect data. The prescription is a three-layer stack whose defended middle layer, the 'enterprise cortex,' holds the company's IP, ontology, and business rules while models and infrastructure above and below stay swappable, governed by workload placement (smallest adequate model, governed fallback) and open protocols like MCP, A2A, and ACP.

themes.theme: Cognitive Lock-In as a New Risk Class

insights.claim: BCG argues that enterprise AI creates 'cognitive lock-in' — a dependency deeper than classic vendor lock-in, in which an organization embeds its data and operational context so thoroughly into a model, platform, or serving stack that switching any of them becomes prohibitively difficult.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Reframes AI vendor risk from a procurement line item into a strategic switching-cost moat; incumbency in the enterprise reasoning layer is worth more than seat-count share.
insights.quote: Cognitive lock-in occurs when an organization thoroughly embeds its data and all of its operational context so deeply into a model, platform, or surrounding operating stack that changing any of them becomes prohibitively difficult.
insights.locator: Why AI Takes Technological Lock-In to a New Level

insights.claim: Contractual data-privacy and ownership protections are insufficient against AI dependency because the exposure is judgment and interpretation, not data — categories that are difficult to define, monitor, or enforce in contracts.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Legal-only AI governance is a false comfort; watch for a new class of technical/architectural controls (routing, evals, ontology layers) as the real spend category.
insights.quote: Strong contracts can protect your data, but exposure to an organization’s data is only part of the issue.
insights.locator: It’s reasonable for a CEO to wonder

insights.claim: Open-weight model deployments do not eliminate lock-in — they relocate it, creating fresh dependencies on a specific checkpoint, tuning pipeline, serving infrastructure, or the internal team that operates it.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'open weights = freedom' pitch; the durable value pools sit in tuning, serving, and ops tooling rather than in weights themselves.
insights.quote: Open-weight deployments can reduce dependence on a provider while creating new dependencies around a particular checkpoint, tuning pipeline, serving infrastructure, or operating team.
insights.locator: This risk is not limited to proprietary frontier models

insights.claim: Cognitive lock-in is described as an emergent outcome of rational behavior by both vendor and customer rather than vendor misconduct, meaning it will not be caught by conduct-based governance or antitrust-style scrutiny.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Implies lock-in accrues quietly and by default — a tailwind for incumbent platform economics that no single decision point will flag.
insights.quote: Cognitive lock-in need not result from misconduct by a provider. It can emerge from perfectly rational decisions by both the provider and the enterprise.
insights.locator: Cognitive lock-in need not result from misconduct

insights.claim: Enterprises are for the first time exposing not just data and business rules to vendors but the reasoning layer above them — how the company thinks, decides, creates, and acts — which BCG calls a genuinely new category of exposure versus decades of ERP and SaaS outsourcing.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The analogy to ERP/SaaS understates the stakes; expect boards to fund a defensive architecture layer that did not exist as a budget line before.
insights.quote: What organizations are now exposing is not just the data and the rules, but the reasoning layer that sits on top of them—how the enterprise thinks, decides, creates, and acts.
insights.locator: It is critical to note that organizations have never before

themes.theme: CEO Question Has Shifted From Model Choice to Commitment

insights.claim: In BCG's conversations with CEOs, the top-of-mind AI question has shifted in recent months from 'Which model should we use?' to 'Are we committing too much, too soon to a single platform?'
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A buying-criteria shift from capability to reversibility favors vendors selling portability and multi-model orchestration over single-stack bundles.
insights.quote: the top-of-mind question for informed CEOs has often shifted from, “Which model should we use?” to, “Are we committing too much, too soon to a single platform?”
insights.locator: Indeed, in our conversations with CEOs

insights.claim: Every major AI platform category — frontier model labs, hyperscalers, and data and software giants — is actively extending into the enterprise's proprietary knowledge layer, making encroachment on customer IP a shared strategic objective rather than a single vendor's behavior.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Expect competitive convergence and margin pressure at the model layer as vendors chase the higher-value context/knowledge layer instead.
insights.quote: Today, providers across the AI ecosystem—from frontier model labs and hyperscalers to open-weight developers and specialist platforms—are racing to own as much of the stack as they can.
insights.locator: No CEO would build a mission-critical supply chain

themes.theme: Observable Warning Signs Before a Technical Audit

insights.claim: BCG offers three non-technical diagnostics that an organization is drifting toward cognitive lock-in: teams can no longer explain 'the why' behind decisions, business leaders complain the AI does not meet actual needs, and strategy starts being shaped around what the model does well.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A cheap, board-level checklist that can be applied to portfolio companies without access to their engineering stack.
insights.quote: When teams begin shaping strategy around what the model does well rather than what the business requires
insights.locator: How can CEOs gauge whether their organization is drifting

insights.claim: The distinguishing test versus prior ERP/SaaS platform dependency is whether the dependency is operational or cognitive — the failure mode is a model that steers the enterprise's thinking rather than merely dictating how work gets done.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete tripwire for assessing whether an AI deployment has crossed from tooling into strategy capture.
insights.quote: Instead of merely dictating how work gets done, the model shapes the enterprise’s thinking to the point where switching it becomes too risky to attempt.
insights.locator: The crucial difference now is that the dependency is cognitive

themes.theme: Three-Layer Stack With a Defended Middle

insights.claim: BCG prescribes a three-layer AI stack — a human and agent access layer on top, an enterprise intelligence layer (the 'enterprise cortex') in the middle, and a platforms and infrastructure layer beneath — with the middle layer owned by the enterprise and the outer two rentable from vendors.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Defines where enterprise AI budget will concentrate: ontology, rules, and orchestration in the middle, commoditizing what sits above and below it.
insights.locator: The AI tech stack has three essential layers

insights.claim: The enterprise cortex is defined as a company's IP, essential data, key business rules, proprietary information, and codified understanding of how processes link to strategy, purpose, and values — an asset class distinct from both data and models.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Names a new balance-sheet-adjacent intangible; vendors that can help codify it (graph DBs, ontology, orchestration) capture the defensible spend.
insights.quote: It’s your IP, essential data, key business rules, proprietary information, and codified understanding of how processes work and how they link to your core business strategies, purpose, and values.
insights.locator: What is your organization’s enterprise cortex?

insights.claim: The access layer should draw on a governed portfolio of models — spanning small language models, open-weight models, and frontier LLMs — selected per task, with common routing, evaluation, and fallback logic keeping the portfolio modular without exposing the cortex.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Multi-model routing and eval infrastructure becomes mandatory middleware, not an optimization — a durable niche between the labs and the enterprise.
insights.locator: The Human and Agent Access Layer

insights.claim: The division of labor BCG recommends is that the model supplies language and reasoning while the enterprise's own layer supplies compliance constraints, permission structures, audit trails, business logic, and definitions that stay consistent from one prompt to the next.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Consistency and auditability, not raw model quality, become the gating factor for putting agents into consequential workflows like pricing and approvals.
insights.quote: Let the model handle language and reasoning, but let your enterprise cortex handle the rules, limits, and consequences.
insights.locator: Set the Parameters for What Is Possible

themes.theme: Live Enterprise Deployments of the Cortex Pattern

insights.claim: A global entertainment company runs an agentic marketing-asset platform in which each creator's voice, brand guidelines, and preferences are codified inside the company's own layer while multiple technology providers' models sit on top drawing context from that single shared layer.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Concrete proof that multi-vendor model portfolios over a shared context layer are already in production, not theoretical architecture.
insights.quote: The result: a frontier LLM scales the creator’s unique ideas to millions of fans, while the sensitive material that defines them remains owned and protected.
insights.locator: A global entertainment company built an agentic platform

insights.claim: In a major retailer's frontline-associate deployment, BCG asserts that an unguarded LLM agent costs more at the register than it delivers in productivity because of hallucination, and that the enterprise cortex functions as a GPS over the company's own data and rules to raise answer accuracy.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The ROI case for grounding infrastructure is negative-without-it, not incremental — a strong argument for retrieval/ontology spend in frontline retail AI.
insights.quote: But LLMs answer on the basis of probabilities, and are prone to hallucinations, so an unguarded agent will cost you more at the register than it will deliver in improved productivity.
insights.locator: A major retailer uses AI to boost frontline associates

insights.claim: A global beauty company has encoded decades of brand standards, retail expertise, and experimentation directly into a company-governed layer that remains portable across models, so the AI speaks in the brand's voice and the institutional expertise cannot leave with departing staff.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Points to knowledge-codification as a retention/continuity play — a second, HR-side justification for cortex spend beyond vendor risk.
insights.quote: The payoff: the AI speaks in the brand’s voice, not in a generic one, and the expertise behind it can’t walk out the door.
insights.locator: A global beauty company encodes decades of marketing know-how

themes.theme: Portability Standards and Modularity as Contract Terms

insights.claim: BCG points to open, standards-based protocols — the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent-to-Agent (A2A), and Agent Communication Protocol (ACP) — as the emerging mechanism ensuring models and agents can connect to external tools and to one another.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Protocol support is becoming a procurement checkbox; vendors that resist MCP/A2A/ACP face a widening disqualification risk in enterprise deals.
insights.quote: Various open, standards-based protocols—including the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent-to-Agent (A2A), and Agent Communication Protocol (ACP)—have been emerging to ensure that models and agents can connect
insights.locator: Standards governing exactly this kind of portability

insights.claim: BCG advises enterprises to write support for open, standards-based context interfaces directly into vendor contracts so their environment stays accessible to any model they might adopt later.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: If this becomes standard contract language, it structurally caps the switching costs vendors can accumulate — a headwind to lock-in-based valuation premia.
insights.locator: Keep the Model and Platform Layers

insights.claim: Portability must extend across model classes — not merely across technology providers — so that an organization can swap models, tools, or platforms without redesigning its entire stack or workflow.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Multi-vendor is not enough; architectures that assume one model class (e.g. only frontier LLMs) carry hidden migration cost when economics shift.
insights.quote: Portability should extend across model classes, not just across technology providers.
insights.locator: Keep the Model and Platform Layers

themes.theme: Workload Placement and Model Portfolio Economics

insights.claim: The stated operating principle for model selection is workload placement: use the smallest, least-expensive model that meets a task's quality, latency, and risk bar, with a governed fallback to a stronger model — or a human — when it falls short.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Systematic downshifting of enterprise inference toward cheap models compresses per-token revenue at the frontier even as total volume grows.
insights.quote: use the smallest, least-expensive model that meets a task’s quality, latency, and risk requirements, with a governed fallback to a stronger model—or a person—when it is unequal to the task
insights.locator: The operating principle is workload placement

insights.claim: BCG segments model economics by task shape: frontier models repay their cost on open-ended, low-volume, high-variety work such as novel reasoning and cross-domain synthesis, while SLMs win on narrow, well-defined, high-volume tasks where token economics and easier governance outweigh lost raw capability.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete segmentation of the enterprise inference TAM — the high-volume repetitive tier is the part most exposed to in-housing and price erosion.
insights.quote: Frontier models repay their cost on open-ended, low-volume, high-variety work—novel reasoning, synthesis across domains, and tasks whose shape you can’t predict in advance.
insights.locator: Manage Models as a Portfolio

insights.claim: For data-rich companies, an open-weight model or fit-for-purpose SLM tuned on proprietary data can become a controlled, specialized owned asset, with the in-house-versus-rent decision being task-shaped rather than a blanket policy.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Supports a bifurcated enterprise AI spend: growing internal fine-tuning/serving capex alongside continued frontier API consumption for the long tail.
insights.quote: If a task is repetitive, bounded, and easier to train, it may be a candidate to bring in-house; if it’s varied, exploratory, or rare, keep leveraging frontier capability.
insights.locator: Manage Models as a Portfolio

insights.claim: BCG's ownership rule for the AI stack is to own the content, rent the containers, and buy or build components — including a graph database and orchestration tooling — from the best available, on the premise that tools are replaceable but the corporate brain is not.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: An explicit buy signal for graph/ontology and orchestration tooling as the 'own' layer, versus rented compute and models as the 'rent' layer.
insights.quote: Own the content, rent the containers, and buy or build the components from the best available, including a graph database and orchestration tooling. Tools are replaceable, but the corporate brain should never be.
insights.locator: Stay Clear-Eyed on Vendor Value and Ownership

insights.claim: Protecting the enterprise's proprietary knowledge layer is framed as a CEO-level governance mandate spanning data, technology, risk, and the business — with a named domain-expert owner responsible for validating rules and upkeep — rather than an IT problem.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Budget authority moving from IT to the CEO/board raises deal sizes and lengthens cycles for vendors selling into this layer.
insights.locator: Stay Clear-Eyed on Vendor Value and Ownership

insights.claim: The companies making the biggest AI strides reshape one entire high-value workflow end to end — a full pricing process, service recovery journey, or credit decisioning flow — secure its operating logic, prove financial payback, and then scale outward, rather than accumulating isolated use cases.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Deep single-workflow deployments are the leading indicator of real AI payback; broad shallow pilot counts are a vanity metric to discount.
insights.quote: Focusing means going deep on one workflow that matters, not shipping shallow features across many workflows.
insights.locator: Move Fast Through Focused Execution

insights.claim: BCG frames the current moment as an inflection point at which CEO architecture decisions determine whether AI strengthens or slowly erodes what makes an enterprise distinctive.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Implies dispersion in AI outcomes will come from architecture choices, not model access — a differentiator to probe in management calls.
insights.quote: The decisions that CEOs make at that inflection point may well determine whether AI strengthens what makes their enterprise distinctive or slowly erodes it.
insights.locator: Many companies are reaching or will soon reach a critical juncture
